newsitem.title: USA: Miami judge lets secondhand-smoke lawsuit proceed.
newsitem.headline: Miami judge lets secondhand-smoke lawsuit proceed.

text.p: A judge refused Monday to decertify class-action status in a secondhand-smoke lawsuit by airline flight attendants against the tobacco industry, allowing jury selection to begin in the landmark case.
Judge Robert Kaye also refused the tobacco companies' motion to deny the flight attendants' request for punitive damages in the class-action lawsuit known as Broin v Philip Morris et al.
The judge also denied the industry's request for a summary judgment on allegations that tobacco companies committed fraud and conspiracy.
Kaye ruled on those issues on Friday but the rulings were released only on Monday.

The trial began with industry attorneys and Susan and Stanley Rosenblatt, the husband-and-wife team representing the plaintiffs, vying over comments to the media and how the hundreds of potential jurors expected to be screened for the panel should be questioned.

"We ask that the court issue a gag order directing counsel on both sides not to speak to the press until the trial is over," David Hardy, attorney for Philip Morris Cos. Inc. and Lorillard Inc., said.
Kaye did not immediately rule on the request. To date, he has limited access to some court documents and asked attorneys to be "circumspect" in talking to the press.

The judge, who had expressed concern about losing too many jurors during a trial expected to last several weeks, ordered 18 chairs be made ready for what was expected to be a panel of six jurors and as many as 12 alternates.
In other rulings since Friday, Kaye dismissed two of the defendants in the case, leaving nine defendants.

Dropped as defendants were Dosal Tobacco Co., a small family-owned cigarette maker in Opa-locka, Fla., and United States Tobacco Co., a unit of UST Co. Inc. and the largest seller of snuff and chewing tobacco.
Neither companies' products had been linked to any plaintiff in the case.
Lead plaintiff Norma Broin attended the first day of the trial, sitting in the courtroom's front row with Patty Young, another plaintiff.
Broin, who was using vacation time from her American Airlines flight attendant's job to be at the trial, said she was "ecstatic" to see the case, which was filed in 1991, finally making it to court.

The suit was filed on behalf of some 60,000 flight attendants, themselves non-smokers, who claim they contracted a variety of maladies, including lung cancer, from breathing cigarette smoke on U.S.-based passenger jets.

Broin, 42, lost part of a lung several years ago to surgery for cancer, now in remission. Young, 50, who was a leader of flight attendants' effort to ban smoking on most U.S. flights, suffers from asthma, chronic bronchitis and other ailments she attributes to breathing secondhand smoke.
"I'm overwhelmed with happiness that something's finally happening here," Young said.

Potential jurors were given a questionnaire two weeks ago containing 93 items, including questions about their English literacy, whether they smoke or have tried to quit smoking, whether they allow people to smoke in their cars or homes and whether they believe nonsmoking flight attendants who did not want to breathe cigarette smoke should have sought other work.
Attorneys for both sides reviewed their responses in recent days and met before the trial started to discuss which should be summarily dismissed.
The judge later brought in the first group of potential jurors and introduced them to the attorneys and told them about the case. They then underwent individual questioning.
